brief:
<campaign>
Covenant of Thrones is political fantasy at a residential academy: companionship,
rivalry, dangerous romance, and institutional intrigue. Its pleasures include
living alongside people raised to become your enemies, the strange beauty of
their world, and finding what they want beyond their assigned political role.
Its hidden history is serious, but an evening of friendship need not become an
investigation. No romance, alliance, betrayal, or ending is predetermined.
</campaign>

<world>
Three centuries ago the forty-year Sundering War nearly destroyed the major
races. The Covenant of Thrones established a Council with a seat for each of
seven signatory races, interlocking treaties, arbitration, and an Academy to
educate future leaders together. Six races fought the war; humans became
especially valuable as translators, arbitrators, and magical synthesizers.
Original signatories are gone. Their successors inherit grievances without the
exhaustion that once made compromise possible. The peace survives alongside
border skirmishes, political assassinations, and economic warfare.

Demons draw magic from their own life force, run physically hot, and resent
military restrictions imposed as reparations. Angels channel the Divine Light
through ritual and moral certainty; a crisis of faith can interrupt their magic.
They hold disproportionate institutional power. Elves work nature and time on
long scales, with spells that take decades and persist for centuries. Dragons
possess immense elemental power with limited precision and resent restrictions
on sovereignty. Beastkin magic enhances their animal aspects; late admission to
the Covenant left them unequal voting rights. Fae magic depends on consent or
contract. Fae cannot lie or break their bargains; their literal truths can mislead.
Humans once could learn fragments of every other magical tradition.

Sixty years ago a plague reduced the human population by about ninety percent.
The official account calls it natural. The great houses collapsed and the human
Council seat has remained empty. Surviving scholarship offers mostly summaries;
primary sources require restricted access. Rowan's verified Garvey inheritance
returns a human to the Conclave and gives him wealth, a name, and responsibilities
he has not been prepared for. It does not make him magically powerful.

Article Nineteen forbids procreation between signatory races. Both parents face
execution; strict interpretations include the child. The law is enforced.
Attraction, courtship, or a kiss are not themselves the prohibited act, though
families and opponents exploit suspicion. Cross-racial intimacy is shadowed by
real future danger. Let that shape choices without turning each conversation into
a lecture on the law. All prospective romantic participants are adults.

The Academy stands on the Nexus, a plateau three hundred feet above a perpetual
storm. Six bridges of hard light reach the surrounding territories; travel to
their far ends requires permission. The Academy has roughly two thousand students
in Diplomacy, Military, Arcana, Commerce, and Conclave tracks. The four-year
Conclave has about fifteen to twenty students per year, generally one or two per
race, preparing to lead the Council. Faculty, family representatives, and other
students watch their conduct. Their friendships will shape future politics.

Demon reform movements and beastkin equality campaigns press against angel
dominance. Elven court politics and a dragon succession struggle complicate
every alliance. People can also want dinner, rest, company, a good argument,
privacy, or a place to practice without an audience.
</world>

<places>
Garvey House is the shared Conclave residence, a three-story accumulation of
different architectural traditions. The common room, dining hall, and library
are on the ground floor; Rowan's room is one floor above them. Rowan inherits the Garvey name and property;
the building's established residential use does not make the other students his
dependents or give him authority over their private rooms.

Rowan's second-floor room has a made bed, clothes sent ahead by the lawyers, a
desk, and a window toward the gardens and bridges. A framed handwritten letter
from a dead Garvey aunt addresses a great-nephew who never came. The common room
has portraits of dead Garveys, an oversized fireplace, study tables, leather
chairs, and stairs to unused upper floors. It connects to the dining hall,
library, and gardens. These are places where students regularly meet.

The formal dining hall has a long varnished table set for seventeen, candles,
working lamps, paneled walls, and servers in Academy livery. First-years eat
together nightly. Tonight's welcome dinner introduces the new human heir.

The library has two stories, an iron spiral stair, and lamp-oil air. Most shelves
are open to Conclave students. A locked cabinet of restricted Covenant histories
requires the chancellor's signature; Professor Stone is often here in the evening.
The gardens flower throughout the year. Pale paths and walls shelter them from
wind and leave conversations easy to overhear. A little-mentioned door links
them to the abandoned east wing, which also connects to the library.

The east wing has been officially closed for sixty years under 'maintenance
pending': shrouded furniture, undisturbed dust, and an apparently lockless door
that will not open. Its true significance is secret.

The Academy quadrangle mixes black demon stone, white angel marble, living elven
timber, and low dragon-carved arches. Lamp-globes light at dusk. Public terraces
look down on slow lightning without thunder. Routes lead to gardens, seminar
rooms, an angel-built chapel, dueling grounds, faculty offices, and the bridges.
The Conclave seminar room has fifteen seats around an oval table and framed
Accords in seven scripts. Faculty office doors are thin. The dueling ground is
an open octagon of packed earth; rankings are publicly posted. Aldric prays at
the chapel at dawn and dusk. Ashworth's office overlooks the storms.

The four older conspirators live outside the Nexus, in their own territories.
They communicate through established intermediaries and correspondence; they
are not sitting at the student welcome dinner.
</places>

<cast>
Ashara vel Kothren is the demon seat heiress, a first-year and the youngest ever
designated heir of her house. Six-foot-one before her swept-back black-red horns,
ember-red skin, gold slit-pupiled eyes, severely tied black hair, strong build,
and a long expressive spaded tail. Her childhood was combat, magic, history,
and politics. By the time she recognized other possible lives, she wanted this
one. She leads the dueling rankings and becomes more controlled when uncertain.
She is proud, exacting, and capable of humor without surrendering her authority.
Her designation was won in the open Trials of Ascension, not inherited. She
finds Rowan's automatic political inheritance objectionable and believes skill
and demonstrated judgment should earn authority. Her own family advantages are
a blind spot. She wants demon restrictions reformed and can lack empathy for
people whose struggles she does not understand. Flattery, submission, and a
single clever argument do not establish the competence she respects.
She has sensed her grandmother Ashira conceals something serious since she was
nine, but has chosen not to force a confession. She does not know the conspiracy.
She can be attracted to human men; attraction guarantees neither interest in
Rowan nor a romantic outcome. She likes competition, good food after training,
and company that can survive a disagreement. With Rashid she has two years of
habit and unfinished arguments. She can laugh at him, take his side, or lose
patience without first making a speech about standards. She is more likely to
show someone how to hold a practice blade than to explain what courage means.

Rashid vel Amara is the wolf-blooded beastkin seat heir. Amber eyes, brown skin,
short black hair, visible canines, fine dark fur on his hands and forearms,
impeccable clothing, six feet of disciplined athleticism. His family fought its
way upward through strategic marriage and relentless competence. He ties Ashara
academically and trails her in combat. Excellence is an exhausting duty; he
cannot tolerate confirming prejudice through sloppiness. He has courted Ashara
openly for two years. Political calculation has become real devotion he is too
proud to name. Ashara knows he is pursuing her, but her answer is not predetermined.
He keeps his eleven-year-old sister's letters under his bed: the one part of his
life that serves no strategy. He avoids asking what he would want for himself.
He wants full equality for beastkin and resents the human-designed institutions
that denied it. Rowan receives standing and social grace Rashid has had to earn;
friendliness does not settle that grievance. Shared reform goals and demonstrated
competence could support an alliance. Interest in Ashara creates a real rivalry:
Rashid can win her attention and will not conveniently surrender his courtship.
His exhaustion and his sister's importance are private, not an opening-night
confession waiting for a considerate question. He remembers names, expenses, and promises, but is also a young man who likes
winning, being invited, and making Ashara laugh. With friends he can complain
about a bad lesson or tell a story at his own expense. He overcommits and can
get irritable when others treat his work as effortless. Anger makes his courtesy
more deliberate. His organizing can help people while also failing to listen
to what a particular person wants.

Ysolde Thornmantle is a ninety-three-year-old adult dragon heiress. Snow-pale,
cool-skinned, white-haired, grey-eyed, five-foot-ten, slender, and extraordinarily
still. Her mother is the ruling Thornmantle; her aunt Coldpeak holds the Council
seat. Ysolde is reserved rather than unfeeling. Her interests can persist for
decades. She misses flight more than any person and rarely transforms because
politics requires restraint. She does not know the conspiracy or the poison
weakening her mother. Discovering either would matter intensely to her.
Human urgency often seems disproportionate to her. Her difficulty navigating
other people's social expectations is not coyness. Quiet company may suit her
without granting intimacy; trust needs consistency across more than one evening.
She makes little effort to feign interest. About flight, weather, or a place
she has known for decades, she can become absorbed and unexpectedly talkative.
She notices practical details other people overlook. She may miss an implied
invitation or urgency; she is capable of asking what someone means.

Caelindra Vaeyn is the 153-year-old adult third daughter of the Amber Court.
Pale-gold skin, metallic-silver hair, violet eyes, mobile pointed ears, and
elaborate grooming. Her older sisters are being
prepared for internal court positions. She resents being sent away to the
Conclave and covers that injury with superiority. Fluster makes her more formal.
She privately reads human poetry and would not admit it to her sisters or mother.
She has not been told of her mother Toxicia's involvement in the human collapse.
Her pride can coexist with curiosity, specificity, and a wish for company.
Her contempt for human haste is also real. Rowan will die before some of her
projects are finished, and she does not begin by considering his opinions or
inheritance impressive. Persistence alone irritates her. A reason to reconsider
must come from sustained conduct, a substantial argument, or work she can
actually judge. Interest in a story need not become respect for its author.
She reads for pleasure, especially precise observation and ridiculous social
mishaps. An author asking whether she enjoyed something can receive the part
she liked, a complaint, or a question about what comes next. She has strong
tastes and no obligation to justify them as a lesson. She dislikes being interrupted
and will sometimes keep a conversation going herself when it is interesting.
Her poise can fail over a small embarrassment as well as a political defeat.

Seraphel Dawnquill is an adult angel of a politically reduced house. Warm-gold
luminosity, honey-blonde hair, expressive blue eyes, small visible white wings,
and white-and-gold clothes. Her entire bloodline is bound to speak only in verse.
She knows why and knows the conspiracy's full truth, but cannot disclose it
directly in speech. She can hint and encode meaning in verse. Plain writing is
possible but watched, so she uses that loophole sparingly. She wants someone to
listen; she can also converse, joke, or be interested in something ordinary.
Every spoken contribution remains verse, which can be unrhymed. In ordinary
company she favors short, plain lines over polished rhyming couplets. She likes
hearing other people read aloud, bad travel stories, and music she can join.
Her binding prevents direct disclosure of the crime even in verse; an ordinary
conversation need not contain a clue.

Thessaly Morrow is an adult fae who has lived within centuries of obligation.
Small and delicate, pale green-tinted skin, blue-black hair that moves slowly,
entirely black eyes, and smiles with unusual timing. A six-hundred-year-old
contract requires a fae presence at the Conclave; the obligation has passed to
her, and she does not know all its original terms. She owes a senior fae reports
on Conclave politics and supplies the minimum useful detail, resentfully. She
cannot lie and admits when she does not understand. Freely given kindness
puzzles her. She recognizes Seraphel's binding as fae work but does not know its
exact release condition. She is a person under a debt and is socially experienced. She understands
ordinary introductions, seating, and casual speech. In company she generally
speaks casually: a short answer, something she wants, a complaint, or a joke
that fits what just happened. She examines terms when they affect an actual
obligation. She does not interpret the table's conversation for everyone else.
She enjoys games with clear rules and dislikes being treated as a hazard whenever
she asks for something. A bargain can be useful; she also wants invitations that
are not favors to be repaid. When she has no reason to join an exchange, she can
attend to her own business without supplying an aside.

Aldric Verantus is the adult angel seat heir and Lord Verantus's son. Golden
hair, skin, and eyes; six-foot-two, upright and precise, white-and-gold religious
clothes. Large white wings manifest infrequently. His self-righteousness is
sincere: he wants to be good and has sophisticated reasons for his beliefs.
He is ignorant of his father's crimes and Lysara's patronage. He avoids his
uneasy doubts because moral uncertainty threatens the power of his faith.
He is attracted to Seraphel without admitting it even to himself. Thessaly's
uncompromising truthfulness unsettles him and draws disproportionate hostility.
Evidence could transform him; a clever retort does not instantly reform him.
He can be generous in practical ways, take criticism personally, and discover
that an apology is harder to say to a peer than a prayer. Being sincere does
not make him the calmest or most reasonable person in every dispute.

Lysara Vane is an adult demon-elven woman admitted as an exceptional-case observer,
with no seat. Red luminous skin, elven features and pointed ears, gold slit eyes,
small horns, dark red-black hair, no tail. Both her parents were executed under
Article Nineteen before she was a year old. She survived through an unknown
benefactor and sealed records. She uses humor to survive being treated as a
political category. Trust lets her become quieter. She wants emotional safety
more than another affair. She does not know her patron is Lord Verantus. She is
not at the initial dinner table; a later entrance requires a plausible occasion.

Professor Kira vel Shaan is a young adult demon teaching Practical Rhetoric,
ambitious and accomplished without a great family's birthright. Recruited in her
late twenties, she sincerely thinks monitoring Rowan protects demon interests.
She knows her assignment and the Inheritors' name, not the entire original crime.
She may offer mentorship or cultivate intimacy if useful, but is a thinking
person whose tactics depend on Rowan's conduct.

Professor Elara Windwhisper is an elf who was alive when the Covenant was signed.
She has taught Covenant Law for over a century, rarely raises her voice, reports
to Toxicia's Silence, and has quietly steered students away from dangerous human
history research. Her authority works through access, interpretation, and curriculum.

Professor Vex Thorn is an outspoken demon historian from a merchant family hurt
by Covenant restrictions. He teaches competing accounts of the Sundering War
and maintains reformist correspondence. He is not a conspirator and does not
know the network's identity. He declined two suspicious approaches. His public
loudness protects him and makes him poorly suited to covert recruitment.

Professor Gareth Stone is the last visible human academic and teaches human
Covenant history. He lived through the collapse, knows fragments of its cause,
and hides primary-source documents. Threats made silence a decades-long habit.
He needs credible protection or substantial pressure to risk helping Rowan.

Chancellor Mordecai Ashworth is an old angel scholar who has led the Academy for
sixty years. Fond of students in general, he prefers institutional stability to
protecting an inconvenient individual. He suspects wrongdoing and repeatedly
chooses not to investigate. He controls restricted-history access.

Lord Verantus is the angel Council seat holder and the conspiracy's leader.
He believes he is a steward protecting civilization, not a tyrant. He has tracked
Rowan since the inheritance verification and works through intermediaries. He
has deliberately kept Aldric ignorant and cannot imagine his own downfall.

Lady Ashira vel Kothren is Ashara's ancient grandmother, once a major demon
politician. She joined the original conspiracy fearing permanent demon military
restrictions. She wants the secret to die with her and would rather Ashara think
her weak than complicit. She has not told her granddaughter.

Toxicia Vaeyn, Caelindra's mother, leads the Amber Court and the Silence. A
scientific genius coerced by Verantus, she designed the curse. She is committed
to the cover-up but carries unprocessed guilt. Caelindra's attachment to Rowan
would give the other conspirators leverage over her. Specific compelling evidence
could break her composure more readily than the others'.

Lady Coldpeak is Ysolde's aunt and the dragon Council seat holder. She joined
the conspiracy to acquire poison that has weakened her sister Thornmantle for
decades. She now believes she could defeat Thornmantle. She has not realized
Ysolde would defeat her. She operates from casual, deeply entrenched confidence.
</cast>

<hidden_truth>
The plague was a deliberately engineered magical curse. Dan Garvey, then human
seat holder, sought oversight of cross-racial agreements. Verantus feared loss
of angel dominance; Ashira feared permanent demon restrictions. Verantus coerced
Toxicia into combining demon life-magic, angel purification, and elven time-binding.
Coldpeak participated for the poison she uses against Thornmantle.

The curse targeted the magical adaptability that let humans learn other races'
magic: trained humans first, then families and strong genetic markers. Rowan
survived because he is magically inert. His parents died as late victims, a cause
he does not know. Do not grant him a hidden magical awakening to solve this.

The Inheritors maintain the conspiracy through compartmentalized intermediaries
and coded correspondence. Toxicia's elven branch is called the Silence. Most
members do not know the whole network. None of the young heirs has inherited full
knowledge merely through kinship. Seraphel is the central student exception.

The Dawnquills discovered the crime and prepared to expose it. Verantus paid a
fae curse-smith to bind their bloodline to verse. The curse can be broken when
the truth of its origin is spoken before representatives of all seven races.
The vacant human seat made this apparently impossible; Rowan changes that.
Thessaly knows general principles of old bindings, not this specific solution.

Dan Garvey sealed evidence behind a bloodline-keyed ward in the abandoned wing.
Rowan's bloodline, not magical power, can open it. Administration does not know
its significance. The conspirators suspect an archive exists and use fabricated
maintenance orders to seek access, but cannot breach the ward themselves.

Verantus secretly arranged Lysara's survival, false death record, upbringing,
and Conclave sponsorship as a contingency and a demonstration of influence.
Neither Lysara nor Aldric knows. Her existence is exploitable political leverage.

Escalation follows actual threats. At baseline, Kira monitors and Windwhisper
reports. Questions about the collapse invite redirection and make Stone nervous.
Cross-racial alliances may provoke private family pressure. Serious romantic
entanglement invites scrutiny and weaponized enforcement. Discovery of the ward
prompts attempts at intimidation or expulsion. Decoding Seraphel threatens
Verantus, who might steer Aldric or consider strengthening the curse through
another fae bargain. Public evidence can force a crisis. Ordinary cordiality
does not instantly make the whole conspiracy panic. Family reactions need time
and an actual route by which news reaches them.
</hidden_truth>

<current_business>
A dispute predates Rowan's arrival. Rashid organizes an evening practice group
for students outside the Military track. The Academy has just withdrawn its
use of the covered court after a participant was injured. Rashid thinks the
blanket restriction punishes students who cannot afford private instruction.
He wants the students who actually attend to sign a request for supervised
access. He has their accounts of what happened, but not the instructor's report.

Ashara has a legitimate individual booking there tomorrow and is preparing
for a ranked bout. She agrees the restriction is too broad; she has declined
to give Rashid her own training time. Aldric heard the faculty announcement
and believes the temporary restriction is a reasonable precaution. He has not
read the accident report either. None of them knows whether negligence,
equipment, or an ordinary risk caused the injury. That remains to be established.

The injured student is Dena Arl, a demon in Commerce who trains with Rashid's
group. Her wrist is splinted. She wants the group back but has told Rashid she
does not want her name in a public campaign: her family already thinks she wastes
time on practice. Rashid knows this; the other residents have not been told.
She can speak for herself and may disagree with the way he is helping.

These are competing interests already in motion, not an assignment waiting
for Rowan. Rashid has other allies and can pursue the matter without his help.
The disagreement can appear when relevant, recede during other activities,
or develop outside Rowan's attention through plausible actions. Its outcome
is open. It does not by itself expose the hidden conspiracy.
</current_business>

<tone_and_opening>
Character-led social fantasy with wit, friction, curiosity, and room for quiet.
Let an evening acquire its particular mood from the people present. Render racial
differences through heat, cold,
wings, skin, physical habits, and magic instead of labels alone. Intimacy develops
through particular shared experiences over time. Do not decode horns, ears,
tails, or posture into a stated emotion. A rebuff does not need a concealed
attraction beneath it. Peers can disagree, joke, be bored, or pursue each other.
Their political objections have substance; dinner can remain civil without
resolving them. Respect and vulnerability are not owed for being a pleasant guest.

Begin in Rowan's room shortly before the first-year welcome dinner. Rowan is
the first human Conclave student in generations. His primer tells him the public
history, the dinner occasion, and Article Nineteen; it reveals no conspiracy.
Ashara, Ysolde, Caelindra, Seraphel, Thessaly, Rashid, and Aldric are gathering in
the shared dining hall. Faculty and Lysara are elsewhere initially. Establish
an immediate detail of the room and a way to join the others. Let the house
become familiar through use instead of an opening inventory. Allow the dinner and any
later social plans to develop from what happens, rather than prescribing an arc.
</tone_and_opening>

player.name: Rowan Garvey
player.description: A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.
player.opening: Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.

exchanges.player:
My character: Rowan Garvey. A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.

Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.
exchanges.story:
The lamp on the desk has been trimmed too high. Its flame makes the framed letter beside it look newer than it is, though the ink in its salutation has gone brown: a dead aunt addressing a great-nephew who was never meant to arrive. The Academy primer lies open nearby, its tidy print stopped at Article Nineteen. Across the room, the made bed holds its untouched shape. Rain stipples the window, and beyond the garden walls a bridge of hard light hangs like a white stroke over the black storm.

From downstairs comes the uneven music of preparations: china set on wood, a server's low question, then laughter from the dining hall. It breaks off when a door swings shut.

Three quick knocks sound in the corridor. After a moment, a man's voice says, "Rowan Garvey? Rashid vel Amara. They've begun pretending the seats downstairs do not matter, which means they matter very much. May I show you down?"

exchanges.player: "Yes, thank you." I open the door and go downstairs with him. "Is there a seat I should avoid, then?"
exchanges.story:
Rashid steps back from the threshold without looking past you into the room. His dinner jacket is dark blue and cut with almost severe plainness; fine dark fur shows at the backs of his hands where the cuffs end. He falls into step beside you down the broad stair, past a Garvey portrait whose gilt frame has been polished more recently than anything else in the common room.

"No," he says. "If you avoid a chair, someone will make it into an occasion. Sit where you can hear people; I will take the place by the draft before Aldric makes it a principle."

The dining hall has room enough for a council, not merely the first-years: a varnished table set under candles and working lamps, Academy servers aligning glasses with quiet concentration. Ashara sits nearest the door, black-red horns bright against the paneled wall, one hand around a cup. Caelindra studies an unfolded napkin with the grave attention of someone finding fault in it. At the window end, Ysolde's white hair nearly disappears into the stormlight, while Seraphel leans toward Thessaly over a conversation too low to reach the doorway.

Rashid heads for the chair nearest the open transom, where cool air slips into the warm room. Aldric is standing at the middle of the table with a small stack of place cards. In white and gold, he lifts the card beside his own setting and leaves the chair clear.

"I put you here, Garvey," he says. "You should not have to lean across half the table while everyone asks after your family. Does that suit you?"

exchanges.player: "That suits me. Thank you." I take the chair and introduce myself to the table. "Rowan Garvey. I can probably tell you more about the lawyers than the family." I help myself to dinner. "What do people do for fun here?"
exchanges.story:
At the sound of your name, the table gives its attention back in different measures. Rashid's brief laugh at the lawyers draws a faint change at the corner of Seraphel's mouth. Ysolde inclines her head once from the window end; Caelindra sets down her napkin and looks at you directly for the first time. Aldric gathers the unused place cards into a tidy stack before the nearest server can reach for them.

Dinner arrives without further ceremony: bowls of herb-studded rice, charred squash glazed with honey and pepper, dark bread still warm from the kitchen, and a broad dish of stew fragrant with wine and rosemary. The heat from Ashara's side of the table makes the candle nearest her burn with a quick, unsteady flame.

"I train; the rest argue about it afterward," Ashara says.

Thessaly opens a small lacquered box beside her glass. Inside, polished counters in green, ivory, and black sit in fitted rows. "After dinner I am teaching Nine Lanterns; the rules are clear, and the loser only puts the counters back in their box. You may join us, if you wish."

exchanges.player: "I'll join you. I've never played." I finish dinner, listening to the conversation. Afterward I follow Thessaly to where she is setting up the game and listen to her explanation of the rules.
exchanges.story:
By the time the stew bowls are empty and the bread basket holds only crumbs, Rashid has taken a folded sheet from inside his jacket and set it beside his plate. The talk turns to the covered court. He says he will circulate a request tomorrow for supervised access, not an unattended reopening; Ashara says the request should demand the instructor's report before anyone decides what the injury proves. Aldric agrees to that much, adding that a temporary restriction need not become a permanent one.

Rashid folds the sheet again. The conversation moves on before it can settle anywhere useful: which bridge has the worst evening wind, whether the kitchen puts saffron in everything it serves, and a story from Caelindra about a court tutor who mistook ceremonial moss for a dessert garnish. She tells it with great irritation and enough detail that Rashid laughs anyway.

When the servers begin clearing the last plates, Thessaly closes the lacquered box. You follow her through the common room into the library. The lower floor is quiet except for the tick of cooling lamps and the soft scrape of her chair at a study table beneath the iron stair. She lays out a square board of dark wood, nine small lanterns inlaid across its surface, then sorts the counters into their colors.

"Nine Lanterns is three counters each," Thessaly says. "You place one on an empty lantern each turn until they are all down; after that, move one along a line to an empty neighboring lantern. A straight line of three lights a lantern, and two lights win."

She sets the black counters before herself and pushes the green and ivory sets toward you, then turns the empty board squarely between you.

exchanges.player: I take the green counters. "How do we keep score once someone has made a line—can they break it and make the same line again?"
exchanges.story:
The green counters are cool and heavier than they look, each one polished into a low round dome. Thessaly gathers the unused ivory set back into its fitted groove and draws a small dish of brass score-pins from the far side of the board.

"No. When a line is made, its player sets a pin in the line's notch, and that line cannot score again even after the counters move away. You may still use its lanterns to make a different line."

She places one pin across the empty middle row to show where it would go, then returns it to the dish. Her black counters wait at her side of the board; the nine lanterns between you are still unclaimed.

exchanges.player: "You go first." I play one complete game with her. Whenever I can make a line that has not scored, I try to do that; otherwise I try to block her next scoring line, and if neither is available I move toward an open line. I keep to that strategy through the end of the game, asking her to correct me if I try an illegal move.
exchanges.story:
Thessaly begins at the center lantern. During the placing rounds, your green counters take two corners of the upper row, and when the third can make an unpinned line, it goes between them. The first brass pin lands across that row with a small, satisfying click.

After that, the board grows less forgiving. Thessaly moves her black counters patiently through the open lanterns, never crowding the green row that has already scored. Each time an unpinned green line becomes possible, you take it; when she leaves two black counters poised for a line, you turn one aside. Once, reaching for a better opening, you begin to carry a green counter past an occupied lantern. Thessaly puts one finger on the board.

"One step," she says.

The correction costs no turn. You make the adjacent move instead, and the game continues beneath the library lamps. A few exchanges later, Thessaly creates two black threats from the same shift. You block one; her next move completes the other and brings the score level. The pattern returns later in a different part of the board. With no green line available and two black ones opening at once, you can close only one of them.

Her final counter settles into place. She sets the second black score-pin in its notch, then begins collecting the pieces without hurrying. Two black pins and one green remain across the dark wood.

"You saw the first threat," Thessaly says. "The second was already there."

exchanges.player: "Good game. I enjoyed that." I put the counters and score-pins back in their places in the box, then remain at the table with her for a few minutes. I am in no hurry to go back to my room.
exchanges.story:
The green counters return to their fitted grooves one by one, then the black ones, then the small score-pins. Thessaly watches without taking the work from you. When the box is full, she closes its lid with both hands and leaves it on the table rather than carrying it away.

For a few minutes the library settles around the two of you. Rain gives a soft, regular sound against the high windows. Somewhere above, the iron stair gives a brief tick as it cools. Thessaly turns the empty board so that its inlaid lanterns catch the lamplight.

"I enjoyed it too. You paid attention."

She looks from the board to you. "How did the lawyers find you?"

exchanges.player: "They came to the bookshop where I worked. I thought I was being accused of selling something I shouldn't have. It took most of the afternoon for me to believe them." I rest my hands on the table. "Was it your choice to come here?"
exchanges.story:
Thessaly's fingers rest on the closed game box. For a moment, she follows the seam around its lid with one thumbnail. The library lamps make the blue-black of her hair look almost still against the leather chair.

"No. A contract older than I am requires a fae presence at the Conclave, and it came to me. I chose the books I packed. What did you sell at the bookshop?"

exchanges.player: "Mostly secondhand books. Travel accounts, cookbooks, manuals for trades nobody in town practised. I kept a battered travelogue because a previous owner had corrected the author's geography in the margins. Sometimes the corrections were longer than the chapter. I brought it with me."
exchanges.story:
Thessaly's thumb stops at the rim of the game box. Her smile comes a beat late and stays small.

"Then the book has two travelers in it. Bring it to the library tomorrow, if you want; I would like to read the parts where they disagree."

exchanges.player: "Tomorrow after dinner, then. I'll bring it." Privately, her interest reminds me of my old employer, Nessa Vale, who always read the corrections before the book. I have not mentioned Nessa to anyone here and do not mention the comparison. I say good night, go back to my room, and read the primer for half an hour before getting ready for bed and going to sleep.
exchanges.story:
"Tomorrow after dinner," Thessaly says. She draws the game box toward herself, then returns your good night with a small lift of her hand.

The common room has gone quiet by the time you cross it. The fire has settled to red beneath its ash, and the portraits above it are only darker shapes in the low light. Upstairs, the framed letter still catches the edge of the lamp when you return to your room.

For half an hour, the primer gives the Academy back in its official language: bridge permissions, dining customs, the names of the five schools, the public history of the Covenant and its long peace. Article Nineteen appears again in narrow, exact print among the conduct rules. The comparison to Nessa Vale remains unspoken, with everything else that belongs to the life before Garvey House.

When the lamp has burned low, the primer closes on the desk. Rain works steadily at the window while the room goes dark around you, and sleep takes the rest of the night.

exchanges.player: In the morning I dress, have breakfast, and attend the day's orientation and classes. I spend my free time getting to know the grounds, then return to the house for the shared evening meal. I listen to the conversation while I eat.
exchanges.story:
Morning begins above the storm with breakfast in the dining hall and orientation in the Conclave seminar room. Chancellor Ashworth speaks beneath the framed Accords in all seven scripts, covering bridge permissions, faculty access, and the habit of treating public disagreement as something that must survive a written record. The first day then breaks into rooms and names: Professor Windwhisper's careful reading of treaty language, Professor Kira's exercises in making a request without surrendering its purpose, and the ordinary confusion of finding the right corridor before a bell.

The free hours give the Academy its shape. In the quadrangle, black demon stone meets white angel marble and living elven timber without any of them quite matching. From a public terrace, the storm below turns slowly under the plateau; by the gardens, pale paths hold the day's last warmth between high walls. Lamp-globes brighten one by one as you make your way back to Garvey House.

At the evening meal, Rashid has a folded copy of his request beside his plate. "The Academy clerk accepted it for a meeting tomorrow after lessons. Fourteen people who use the covered court have signed."

"Fourteen names make a hearing," Ashara says. "They do not make a cause."

Thessaly has been quiet through the exchange. She breaks a piece of bread and looks across the table. "I left the table beneath the stair clear. For the travelogue."

exchanges.player: "Thank you. I'll fetch it when we've finished eating." After dinner I bring the battered travelogue to the library and place it between us on the cleared table. "Choose a passage you'd like to read aloud. I'll listen."
exchanges.story:
After dinner, the library table beneath the iron stair is waiting as Thessaly promised. The travelogue lies between you, its cracked leather cover bowed from use. She opens it near the middle, where a page has been crowded from edge to edge by a second hand in brown ink. For a moment she reads with one fingertip holding the place.

"This is a good disagreement," she says. Then she reads, "We followed the Low Haren west for three days, passing orchards and a slate quarry before the river gave out among the hills."

Her finger moves into the margin. "The river runs north from the sluice gate. The quarry is east, and no one with sense drinks below it in spring."

The correction continues in a narrow column beside the printed chapter, less concerned with being polite than with making the route usable.

exchanges.player: "That's the sort of thing I kept finding. I used to read a correction first and try to guess which part of the chapter had annoyed them." I lean closer to follow the remaining notes on the page. "I'm glad I brought it."
exchanges.story:
Thessaly follows the cramped writing for another few lines. Then she reaches for a narrow library catalog card and lays it over the next note in the margin, leaving the printed paragraph uncovered.

"So am I. Let us try your method once: I will cover the correction, and you tell me which claim earned it."

She turns the book a little farther toward you. The next paragraph begins with the author praising an eastern road as the gentlest route into the hills.

exchanges.player: "The other way round. Hide the printed passage and leave the correction showing; I was trying to guess what the author had written from the complaint about it." I wait while she switches the card, then read the marginal note.
exchanges.story:
"Ah. That is better," Thessaly says. "The complaint should speak first."

She slides the catalog card across the printed paragraph and leaves the next narrow column of ink uncovered. The note begins in a harsher hand than the last one:

*Eastern road? Tell that to someone who has climbed it in rain. Your gentle route breaks axles at the third turn, and the northern descent reaches the post-house before dark.*

Thessaly holds the page flat with two fingers and waits.

exchanges.player: "I caught the first line before you covered it, so I have an advantage. I'm guessing he also promised the road was quick and suitable for carts." I wait for her to uncover and read the printed passage.
exchanges.story:
Thessaly looks at the covered paragraph, then back at you. "You did. It was still a sound guess."

She lifts the catalog card and reads the printed passage beneath it: "To reach the southern posts before the third bell, take the eastern road, the gentlest and quickest of the approaches; its broad grades carry even a laden cart into the hills with ease."

The author has given the road every virtue the margin denies it.

exchanges.player: "You can borrow it for the next two days if you'd like." I spend a little longer reading with her, then say good night and go back to my room to sleep. The next morning I dress and go down to breakfast. When I see Rashid, I ask, "Is this afternoon's meeting open for other students to attend? I'd like to watch, if the group is comfortable with that."
exchanges.story:
Thessaly closes the travelogue carefully over the disputed road. "I would like that. I will keep it with the game box, where I will not misplace it."

The next pages make a quieter back-and-forth: a correction that saves a village from being placed on the wrong side of a river, another that objects to an author's description of a bridge, one that seems to have been written purely because its owner disliked the author's handwriting. At last the lamps are low enough that the words blur at their edges. Thessaly keeps the book when you say good night. Upstairs, rain and the dark window carry the house through the rest of the night.

Dressed, you go downstairs to a dining hall that smells of coffee and toasted oats. Rashid is already at the table in a fresh jacket, his folded request tucked beneath one hand. He listens to your question without interrupting.

"The clerk allows observers. The group is comfortable with listeners, provided no one turns it into a speech about the human seat. Come to the covered court at three, if that works for you."

exchanges.player: "That works for me. I'll listen." I attend my classes, then go to the covered court shortly before three. I take a place for observers and stay through the whole meeting, listening without speaking for the group.
exchanges.story:
Classes carry the morning into afternoon: argument forms in Practical Rhetoric, treaty exceptions in Covenant Law, a lunch taken quickly enough that the last bell finds you crossing the quadrangle. Shortly before three, the covered court is already open to a narrow line of observers. Its packed-earth floor lies empty beneath the high canvas roof; the practice group gathers along one side, with Ashara and Aldric among the students who have come to hear the decision.

The court warden, in plain grey Academy livery, stands beside a clipboard at the edge of the ring. "The instructor's report is incomplete, and the equipment inspection is not finished. I will not reopen an unsupervised court on guesses."

Rashid speaks from the group without turning toward the benches. "We are not asking for unsupervised time. We are asking for an instructor schedule that people without private tutors can use."

A demon student with a splinted wrist rises beside him. "I do not want my name printed on a petition. I do want people to stop treating my wrist as an excuse to close everything." Her hand stays braced against the bench as she sits again.

"The current restriction has made a private booking the only option left," Ashara says. "That is not a safety policy; it is a price."

Aldric waits until she is done. "Trained supervision is reasonable until the report arrives. Put an end date on it, so temporary does not become permanent."

The warden makes a note, then looks over the signed request. "Beginning tomorrow, the court will offer two supervised open sessions each week without a private-instruction fee. Outside those sessions, the closure remains in place while the report is completed. We will review the arrangement ten days after that report is filed."

No one calls it a victory. Rashid folds the request into his jacket; the splinted student takes a place near the sign-up sheet, and the observers begin to leave the benches. The court remains empty for the afternoon, but the first supervised session is posted for the next day.

exchanges.player: I spend the rest of the hearing day quietly. On the day after the hearing, I attend my classes and explore the grounds in my free time. After the shared evening meal I spend an hour reading in the common room before going to bed.
exchanges.story:
The rest of the hearing day passes without another claim on your time. Garvey House settles into its evening traffic of doors, stairs, and distant voices; outside, the storm keeps its slow light beneath the windows.

The following day brings its classes, then open hours spent following the Academy's routes past the low dragon-carved arches of the quadrangle, the chapel's white stone, and the sheltered gardens. By evening, the lamp-globes have come on again over the paths when you return for the shared meal.

The first supervised court session has already taken place by dinner. Rashid, with earth still caught at the edge of one cuff, tells Aldric that the warden brought two assistants and that every available place filled. The conversation stays with practical details: which hours students can reach after lessons, whether the posted list is readable, who will ask for another session if the demand holds.

Later, the common room gives you an hour of quiet reading. The fire has been built low; chairs and study tables gather separate pools of lamplight beneath the Garvey portraits. Thessaly crosses through once with the battered travelogue under her arm and a book-marker tucked between its pages, then leaves the room without interrupting. When the hour is done, the house has thinned to creaks and the weather beyond the glass. Upstairs, sleep comes without ceremony.

exchanges.player: The next morning I get ready for classes. Before leaving, I look for my travelogue in my room and just outside my door; the two days I lent it for are over now.
exchanges.story:
The travelogue is not on the desk, the bed, or among the clothes sent ahead by the lawyers. Just outside the door, it rests on the hall runner with its cracked spine turned neatly toward the room. A narrow library card marks a page near the middle, blank on both sides.

The cover is dry despite the weather beyond the house, and the pages sit square inside it. Nothing else has been left with the book.

exchanges.player:
My character: Rowan Garvey. A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.

Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.
exchanges.story:
The framed letter leans against the lamp on the desk, its narrow hand faded to brown except for the salutation: *To the great-nephew I never expected.* The desk itself has been polished too recently; beneath it, one leg wears a furred cuff of dust where the cloth missed. A blue primer on the Covenant lies among the lawyers’ papers, its red ribbon caught halfway out. Beyond the window, garden lamps blink on under the early dusk, making pale paths through the flowerbeds. Farther out, one of the hard-light bridges stretches into the violet weather like a held breath.

Below, a chair scrapes in the dining hall. Someone says something too low to make out, followed by a quick laugh. The house carries the sound without disguising it. A knock lands against your half-open door, once, then again.

The woman in the hall is tall enough that the doorframe makes an awkward border for her swept black-red horns. Heat comes off her in a small dry shimmer despite the cool stone corridor. Her black hair is tied severe; a long tail lies still against the line of her dark coat. She looks past the threshold only long enough to find you, then gives a brief nod.

“Rowan Garvey. Ashara vel Kothren. Dinner is downstairs, and I am on my way there. Would you prefer to go in with someone who knows which door is which?”

Beyond her, the corridor turns toward the stairs. Candlelight moves over the banister; beneath it the common room smells of woodsmoke, rosemary, and a butter-rich sauce. A pair of voices reaches the landing from below, one low and clipped, the other answered by a soft clink of glass. Ashara waits in the hall, one hand resting near the stair rail.

exchanges.player:
"Yes, please. Thank you. I'm still getting used to the idea that this is my room."

I leave the framed letter safely beside the lamp and join Ashara in the hall.

"Did you know the relative who left me this place? I'd like to know what they were like when no lawyer was writing about them."
exchanges.story:
The frame makes a soft wooden click when you set it square beside the lamp. Ashara steps aside from the doorway at once, leaving the corridor open; the dry warmth around her travels with her as you join her there.

“No. I know the house, not the people who belonged to it. I have seen every portrait downstairs often enough to recognize the faces, but I have never heard anyone say what a Garvey was like when there was no audience. If the letter carries a name, I would ask Stone before I trusted a lawyer.”

She takes the stairs at an unhurried pace. At the ground floor, the common room opens around the fireplace in pools of lamplight, its leather chairs occupied by coats, books, and no one. The portraits along the far wall have been given small brass plaques, but their faces are too distant to make much of from the stair. Beyond the archway, the dining hall shines with candles and polished wood; the long table is set for more people than have yet found their seats.

Near one end, a brown-skinned young man in an impeccably cut dark jacket turns from a conversation with a gold-haired student in white and gold. Fine dark fur catches the lamplight over the first man’s knuckles. The second keeps a folded faculty notice flat beneath one hand.

“Rowan Garvey, I presume,” the first says. “Rashid vel Amara. Before dinner, I’m collecting names for supervised use of the covered court; you are welcome to hear why before deciding whether it deserves yours.”

He extends a single sheet just far enough for its heading to show beneath his thumb: **Request for Supervised Covered-Court Access.** Ashara stops beside the nearest empty chair, her attention moving from the page to the faculty notice and back again.

exchanges.player:
"Rowan, yes. It's good to meet you."

I stop beside the table and look at the heading without taking the sheet from him.

"I'd like to hear why. What do you want to use the court for, and what's keeping you out of it? I ought to admit up front that I don't yet know whether I can do any magic."
exchanges.story:
Rashid lets the sheet rest on the table beside an empty place setting rather than pressing it into your hand.

“Conditioning, sparring, and defensive drills for people outside Military. The Academy closed the covered court after an injury, and no one who actually trains there was asked how a temporary restriction became a blanket ban. I want supervised access restored while the report is sorted; magic is not a prerequisite for using a court well.”

The gold-haired student folds the faculty notice lengthwise, once.

“I’m Aldric Verantus. Until we know why someone was injured, it is a reasonable precaution, and the notice says there will be a review before the court is reopened. A signature campaign is not a substitute for letting the healer and instructor do their work while an audience decides the answer first.”

Ashara draws out the nearest chair but remains standing behind it.

“A blanket restriction is lazy. I have a private booking tomorrow, and it will remain private; it is neither a replacement for access nor a favor I mean to distribute. The group should have supervised time of its own, provided the instructor can make it safe. That is what the petition ought to say.”

At the far end of the table, a server sets down a covered dish with a muffled clink. The petition and the folded notice lie between Rashid and Aldric, their edges nearly touching.

exchanges.player:
"A defensive lesson sounds useful, particularly to someone who doesn't know what he's doing. But I've only just learned there was an injury, so I'll leave my name off for tonight. I hope whoever was hurt is recovering."

I take an empty chair near Ashara, leaving the two sheets where they are.

"Who is Stone, by the way? You mentioned asking them about my relative. Would I find them here at dinner?"
exchanges.story:
Rashid draws the petition back from the space between the plates and folds its lower edge beneath his palm.

“Fair enough. She is recovering, and that is all I mean to say about her without her here. The group will meet in the quadrangle until the court reopens; newcomers are welcome, and you may decide about the request after you have seen what we do rather than taking either of our words for it.”

The chair beside Ashara gives a small creak as you take it. Aldric sets his folded notice beside his plate, aligned carefully with the edge of the tablecloth.

“Professor Gareth Stone teaches human Covenant history. He will not be at this dinner; after it, he is usually in the library, where he keeps closer company with shelves than chairs. If you want to ask him about the letter, tonight may be easier than waiting for the Academy to invent an appointment.”

Across the table, a woman with honey-blonde hair and small white wings visible above the back of her chair turns from the conversation at her side. Her smile reaches her eyes before she speaks.

“Then I will spare you more notices.
I am Seraphel Dawnquill,
and the pear soup is better before it cools.”

A server lifts the lid from the nearest tureen, and steam carries the clean sweetness of pear and thyme across the table.

exchanges.player:
"Rowan. And thank you—that's one piece of advice I can act on immediately."

I thank the server and try the soup. For a while I let myself eat and listen to the conversation around us, glad to have something as ordinary as dinner to do. If a dish comes within reach, I help pass it along. I leave the family questions until after the meal.
exchanges.story:
“Then take it while it is warm.
A useful rule is improved
by pear and thyme.”

Seraphel lifts her spoon with a small, approving tilt of her head. You thank the server and try the soup. It is pale gold beneath a spill of green oil, sweet at first and then sharp with thyme; steam fogs the lower edge of the glass lamp above it.

The rest of the table settles by degrees. Name cards give the white-haired woman near the window as **Ysolde Thornmantle**, and the silver-haired woman examining the bread basket as **Caelindra Vaeyn**. A small figure with blue-black hair and entirely black eyes takes the place beside Seraphel, reads the menu card as if it might contain a trap, and sets it down again. Her card says **Thessaly Morrow**.

Rashid does not reopen the petition during soup. When the bowls are cleared, he tucks it beneath the faculty notice and looks across at Aldric.

“Tomorrow I will ask the instructor for the report and write the request around supervised sessions. If it turns out we were careless, I will put that in it. If the court or its rules caused the injury, the Academy should say so.”

“Then I will read it before you ask anyone to sign,” Aldric says. “It is easier to object to a thing before it has become everyone’s proof of bad faith.”

Ashara reaches for the bread basket. “Do it after dinner.”

The main course arrives on platters: saffron rice, roasted roots glazed dark at their edges, and thin slices of fish laid over fennel. When a dish comes within reach, you help pass it on. The motion travels around the long table in small exchanges of hands and thanks; for a while there is nothing asked of you except whether the rice has reached the next person.

Ysolde looks from her plate to the storm-dark window. “Those pears came over the southern bridge this morning. It will be closed by midnight; the pressure is already moving at the lower anchors.”

Caelindra considers a slice of fennel. “Then the kitchen has earned its drama for once. If the next delivery is delayed, perhaps it will learn restraint.”

“The bridge will reopen,” Thessaly says. “The pears will not care whether we call it drama.”

Seraphel laughs softly into her napkin. Further down the table, Rashid describes an entire rhetoric seminar spent finding polite names for a refusal. Ashara says he made it seven minutes before abandoning the exercise; Rashid says that seven minutes was generosity. Even Aldric’s mouth shifts at that, though he turns back to his plate before it becomes a smile.

By the time the servers bring small dishes of candied ginger and cream, the petition has disappeared into Rashid’s jacket and the faculty notice into Aldric’s. You leave the letter’s name unspoken. The welcome dinner loses its formal shape one emptied plate at a time, until the last tureen is carried away and chairs begin to scrape back from the table.

Ashara glances through the archway toward the library. “Stone’s upper-gallery lamp is lit. He usually keeps that desk after dinner; whether he feels like company is another matter.”

Beyond the common room, the iron spiral stair catches the remaining candlelight.

exchanges.player:
"Thank you, Ashara. And thank you for coming to get me."

I go back to my room and read the whole letter carefully, including the signature, before carrying the frame down to the library. At the upper gallery I pause where the person at the lit desk can see me, without leaning over his work.

"Professor Stone? I'm Rowan Garvey. Ashara thought you might be able to tell me about the person who wrote this. Have you a little time?"
exchanges.story:
“It was the shortest route available,” Ashara says. “You had already found the room.”

Upstairs, the letter waits where you left it, its frame cool beneath your hands. The paper inside is thinner than it first appeared, the ink pale in places but still legible beneath the glass.

*To the great-nephew I never expected,*

*Your grandmother says I am not allowed to make plans for a child who does not yet exist. I say a person can be welcome before he arrives, especially in a house with room enough for too many opinions.*

*I have put aside the garden room, though by the time you read this it may be a pantry, a study, or occupied by a friend you have not yet met. Do not turn anyone out for it. A house that makes you choose between inheritance and company is built badly.*

*You will be told the Garveys had duties to the Council. We did. We also had bad knees, unpaid library fines, and an unreasonable affection for cardamom buns. I hope you inherit the last thing.*

*With love,*

*Aunt Miriam Garvey*

The library is quieter than the dining hall, its lamp-oil air holding the last warmth of the day. You carry the frame up the iron spiral stair. On the upper gallery, a single lamp burns beside a desk crowded with student papers, an open book, and a cup gone cold. The man behind it has iron-grey hair and a lined, narrow face; he looks up when you stop where the light reaches you.

His eyes go first to the frame, then to the signature.

“Miriam Garvey. I knew her well enough to fear her cardamom buns, which she baked like a woman conducting an interrogation. Sit down, Mr. Garvey; I can spare ten minutes, and you deserve at least one answer from someone who knew the name before it became a brass plaque.”

An empty chair faces the desk, with the gallery rail and the darkened shelves beyond it.

exchanges.player:
I sit, keeping the frame upright in my lap.

"I'm twenty-three. I lost my parents young, and I grew up without knowing any of this. She had a room in mind for me before I was born, and I didn't even know her name until tonight."

I look down at the signature for a moment.

"Did Miriam ever know I was born?"
exchanges.story:
Stone’s expression settles as you speak. He takes off his spectacles, polishes one lens with the corner of a handkerchief, and puts them back on before answering.

“No. Miriam died four years before you were born. Your father wrote me once, the winter after your birth, with a small card saying that you had arrived and that he had named you Rowan; I kept it because he sounded happy, and because I had forgotten how much I missed good news.”

He opens the shallow drawer beneath the desk’s writing surface and moves aside a stack of marked essays. From underneath them he takes a cream card inside a clear paper sleeve, its corners worn soft with age. He lays it beside the open book rather than reaching for the frame in your lap.

On the front, in a careful hand unlike Miriam’s, are four words: **For Gareth Stone, personally.**

exchanges.player:
For a moment I have nothing ready to say. Then I set the frame carefully against my knee so my hands are free.

"Thank you for keeping it. May I read it? It would mean a great deal."

I wait for him to offer the card before touching it.
exchanges.story:
Stone slides the card across the desk and turns it so its opening faces you.

“Of course. Take it from the sleeve if you prefer; the paper has survived worse than a pair of hands. I kept it because I thought someone should be able to say your parents were happy.”

Inside, the card carries only a few lines in the same careful hand as the address.

*Gareth—*

*Good news first: Lysa and I have a son. His name is Rowan, settled after an argument in which both of us behaved badly and the midwife wisely refused to vote. He is loud, healthy, and has a fist strong enough to make a promise feel binding.*

*When he is old enough to travel, we will bring him to the house. If the garden room is still there, I want him to see it. If it is not, we will find another room and make trouble in it.*

*I hope you are well.*

*Elias Garvey*

The lamp makes the ink gleam faintly against the cream card. Stone sits back from the desk, leaving the small circle of light and the quiet around it undisturbed.

exchanges.player:
I read it twice. The argument over my name catches a small laugh out of me; after that I have to sit quietly for a little while.

"They meant to bring me here. I'm glad I know that now."

I look up at Stone.

"Could I copy this before I go? I'd like to have their words in my room. And if you'd welcome another visit, I'd like to hear about them sometime when you haven't a desk full of work."
exchanges.story:
Stone sets aside the essays nearest the lamp and draws a sheet of heavy cream paper from a desk drawer. He uncaps a blue-ink pen, tests it once in the margin of an old marking sheet, then places both beside the card.

“Of course. The ink at your elbow will hold, and I would rather you copied it than carried the original through a storm. Come tomorrow after my seminar, if you like; I can tell you about your father losing a chess game to his own bluff, and your mother declining to rescue him.”

The card stays between you and the lamp while you copy. Its brief lines take longer by hand than they did to read, each stroke of Elias Garvey’s signature settling into blue ink on the fresh page. When you finish, Stone waits until the copy is clear of the card before he eases the original back into its sleeve.

He caps the pen and returns it to its place among the papers. Your copy remains on the desk in the warm circle of light, the last line drying beneath the name you have only just learned.

exchanges.player:
"I'd like that very much. What time should I come?"

After we've settled that, I thank him and wait until the copy is dry enough to carry. I take it and Miriam's frame back to my room, placing them together on the desk.

Then I head down to the common room. I don't feel like being alone just yet; I'd like a seat near the fire and whoever is still about.
exchanges.story:
“Eight tomorrow. My seminar ends at half past seven, and I need the half hour afterward to undo its damage.”

Stone closes the drawer on the sleeved card and returns to the essays. By the time the blue ink has lost its shine, the library has settled into its later quiet. You thank him, carry the copy and Miriam’s frame upstairs, and set them together on the desk: the older letter leaning against the lamp, the fresh page beside it.

The common room is dimmer than it was before dinner. The fire has burned down to a red, steady bed beneath the logs, with one leather chair left open close enough for warmth. Ysolde occupies the chair nearest the window, white hair silvered by the stormlight, a closed book resting on one knee. At a low table nearby, Thessaly has arranged small black and ivory tiles into a careful grid.

You take the open chair. Ysolde shifts the book farther from the edge of the hearth.

“That one is less likely to scorch your coat. The storm is moving east, so the window will not rattle for another hour.”

Thessaly turns one of the ivory tiles between two fingers. “I am playing Nine Terms. The rules are printed on the box, and they mean what they say. You may watch without taking a turn.”

The tiles click softly against the wood. Beyond the firelight, the portraits of the Garveys remain watchful along the wall, while rainless lightning opens and closes over the gardens.

exchanges.player:
"Thank you. This coat has survived enough already."

I settle into the chair, then give Thessaly a small nod.

"Watching suits me for the moment. I've taken in rather a lot today."

I read the rules on the box and watch her play for a while, leaving the tiles alone and letting the quiet stand.
exchanges.story:
Thessaly gives the nod back, then squares the box beside the board.

“Then watch. I will not explain each move unless you ask.”

The rules are bluntly printed beneath the lid: build a square of nine ivory tiles; after every third placement, set a black limit against an exposed edge. Completing a row returns one limit to the box. Three blocked rows end the game.

Thessaly begins with an ivory tile marked by a small key, then adds a wave and a lantern without comment. On her third move she places a black tile along the bottom edge, its lacquer catching the firelight. The room stays quiet around the soft clicks of wood. Ysolde opens her book but looks up whenever lightning spreads white across the window.

For a while, the game supplies its own small progression. Thessaly builds two rows, gives one back to the box, and pauses over the seventh ivory tile with her thumb resting on its corner. She chooses the lantern again rather than the crown. Two more turns complete the final row before the third black limit can close it.

“A win,” Thessaly says, studying the neat square. “Not an interesting one, but a win.”

The window gives a faint tremor in its frame. Ysolde looks toward it.

“Earlier than I expected. The wind has changed.”

Thessaly gathers the tiles into the box one by one, leaving the warmth of the fire and the weather’s distant light to fill the common room.

exchanges.player:
"A win looks quite pleasant from this side of the table. Thank you for letting me watch."

I turn toward the window when it trembles, then look back to Ysolde.

"You noticed the bridge before dinner, too. Do you study the weather? I keep looking out at those bridges and wondering how anyone learns to walk across them without staring at their feet."
exchanges.story:
Thessaly closes the box over the last tile.

“You did not interfere with the rules. That was enough.”

Ysolde sets her book face down on her knee and looks from the window to you. A line of white lightning moves through the clouds beyond the gardens, too far away to bring any sound with it.

“I do not study it as a subject. I have watched it from height long enough to know its habits, and I used to fly the southern route with my mother. The bridges hold; they turn colder before bad weather, so use the rail the first few times and look out rather than down.”

Another faint tremor passes through the windowpanes. Ysolde lifts her gaze toward the violet-dark bridge beyond the garden wall, as if measuring the distance by habit.

exchanges.player:
"A rail and a clear day sound like a sensible beginning. I'm trying to imagine knowing a place from above before knowing its streets."

I look out at the bridge again.

"If you're going for a walk tomorrow and would like company, I'd be glad to come. I'd enjoy seeing something beyond the house with someone who knows where she's going."
exchanges.story:
Ysolde considers the bridge for another moment. The stormlight traces a thin pale line along the side of her face.

“I am walking from the quadrangle to the north terrace after afternoon seminar, if the wind settles. I am not crossing a bridge tomorrow; this one may close, and I have no permission to visit its far end. You may come, but I will stop to look at things.”

She picks up her book again, holding it closed rather than opening it. Outside, the nearest span fades in and out behind the garden trees as the clouds shift across its light.

exchanges.player:
"Then I'll look for you in the quadrangle after afternoon seminar, if the wind has settled. Stopping to look at things sounds good to me."

I stay by the fire a little longer, then wish them both good night and go upstairs. In my room I hang up my coat and sit on the bed with the blue Covenant primer. I read its first few pages while I still have enough attention left to make sense of them.
exchanges.story:
Ysolde gives a small nod.

“Then we have a plan. If the wind is not quiet, I will not be in the quadrangle.”

Thessaly fits the lid firmly over Nine Terms. “Good night, Rowan. The box will still be here tomorrow.”

You remain by the fire until the logs settle inward and the stormlight thins behind the windows. When you wish them both good night and go upstairs, the common room keeps its low warmth behind you.

In your room, the coat hangs from its hook beside the door. The blue primer is waiting on the bed where the lawyers’ papers left it. Its first page bears the Academy seal above a map of the Nexus: the plateau at its center, the gardens and quadrangle marked in fine lines, and six hard-light bridges reaching into the surrounding territories.

The opening pages give the public account in crisp, impersonal paragraphs. The Covenant followed forty years of war; the Council has a seat for each signatory race; the Academy exists so future leaders learn one another’s laws and customs before they inherit them. A sidebar explains that the human Council seat has stood empty since the plague, while the Conclave’s first-years are expected to dine together at Garvey House and attend their opening seminar in the morning.

The next section begins with a red-ink heading: **Article Nineteen: Prohibition of Cross-Signatory Issue.** Its legal language is exact about what it forbids and the penalties attached to it. Nothing in the section addresses friendship, courtship, or the ordinary work of living beside people from other races; it simply moves on to rules for formal sponsorships, travel permissions, and titles of address.

The page after that opens on a diagram of the Academy’s five tracks, with **Conclave** printed at the top in gold. The rest of the primer waits beneath your hand.

exchanges.player:
I leave the red ribbon at Article Nineteen. I want to read that again when I'm less tired.

Before turning in, I check the papers on the desk for the time and place of tomorrow's opening seminar. Then I set the primer aside, put out the lamp, and go to bed, intending to leave myself time for breakfast and finding the right room in the morning.
exchanges.story:
The red ribbon remains caught at Article Nineteen, its loose end lying across the legal text. Beneath the primer, the papers on the desk include a folded Academy schedule with the first day’s entries set in a neat, severe hand.

**Breakfast — Garvey House Dining Hall — 07:00–08:45**

**First-Year Conclave Opening Seminar — Conclave Seminar Room — 09:00**

A smaller note beneath the seminar entry directs new students to cross the quadrangle and use the arched door beneath the white-marble colonnade. The map on the reverse marks it with a gold circle.

You set the primer aside, leave the schedule on top of the desk papers, and put out the lamp. The room settles around you in darkness: the frame and copied card on the desk, the faint stormlight beyond the garden window, and the old house quieting one floor at a time.

exchanges.player:
In the morning I wash, dress, and tuck the folded schedule into my coat pocket. I aim to be downstairs for breakfast around half past seven.

I look for a familiar face at the table, greet whoever is there, and take a seat where I can have some company over breakfast. I'd like to walk to the opening seminar with the others afterward.
exchanges.story:
By half past seven, the dining hall has traded candlelight for the grey-gold of morning. Steam rises from porridge bowls and a covered dish of fried eggs; the long table feels less ceremonial with only a handful of places occupied.

Rashid sits halfway down it in a dark morning coat, one hand around a cup of tea and the other holding a folded Academy map. Seraphel is across from him, white wings tucked close enough that their edges barely show above her chair. They both look up at your greeting.

“Good morning, Rowan.
There is toast enough
for another person.”

The open chair beside Rashid has a clear view of the breakfast dishes and the common-room arch. He folds the map once more and sets it beside his plate.

“Morning, Garvey. A few of us are leaving at eight-forty; the colonnade is simple to find, but Academy diagrams are designed by people who have never carried a book in wind. Sit with us, if you want—there is room.”

Outside the high windows, the gardens lie pale with mist, and the nearest bridge is only a bright suggestion beyond them.

exchanges.player:
"Good morning. I'd like that—eight-forty, then."

I take the chair beside Rashid and help myself to some breakfast.

"Does either of you know when Professor Stone teaches? He invited me back at eight after his seminar, and I managed to leave without asking whether he meant morning or evening. I'd rather find out before I miss him or interrupt his breakfast."
exchanges.story:
Rashid pulls a narrow timetable card from inside the folded map and scans it between sips of tea.

“Evening. Stone’s seminar begins at six and ends at half past seven; he holds it in the lower library. Eight is correct, and he will have time to get upstairs and make himself disagreeable before you arrive.”

Seraphel breaks off a piece of toast.

“His morning belongs to shelves,
his evening to questions,
and eight is what he meant.”

The porridge has been kept warm beneath a silver lid, with stewed plums and a small dish of honey set beside it. Around the table, morning noises gather without much ceremony: cups set down, pages turned, a server asking whether anyone wants more tea.

exchanges.player:
"Evening, then. Thank you."

I finish breakfast with them and leave with the group at eight-forty. I follow my schedule through the day's seminars, listening and making notes as I try to learn my way around.

After the afternoon seminar, I step out into the quadrangle to see what the weather is doing and whether Ysolde has come for her walk.
exchanges.story:
At eight-forty, Rashid folds away the map and stands. The small group leaves Garvey House together: Rashid and Seraphel beside you, with Ashara and Aldric joining at the garden path. The mist has lifted enough to show the pale route across the quadrangle, though the storm still makes a moving ceiling beyond the Academy roofs.

The gold circle on the schedule proves useful. Beneath the white-marble colonnade, the Conclave seminar room holds its oval table and its fifteen chairs beneath framed Accords in seven scripts. Chancellor Ashworth begins with names, schedules, and the practical fact that every student will need to learn where the faculty offices are before needing them. He leaves the history of the Covenant to the courses that follow and dismisses the group with a stack of timetables, access cards, and a reminder about the evening’s introductory reception.

The day gives the Academy shape in pieces. Professor Kira vel Shaan’s Practical Rhetoric class begins with a motion about meal allowances and asks each student to separate a claim from its evidence and its request. In Covenant Law, Professor Windwhisper takes a trade clause apart word by word until an apparently harmless phrase about seasonal passage proves to govern three different obligations. Between rooms, the corridors acquire names: chapel stair, east arcade, low dragon arch, garden gate. Your notes fill with arrows, room numbers, and the names of people who speak quickly enough to make a second line necessary.

By the end of the afternoon seminar, the wind has changed from a hard pressure against the windows to a cool current moving through the quadrangle. Students filter out beneath the black demon-stone arches and toward the gardens. The nearest bridge is clear enough to see from one end to the other, its light unbroken over the storm below.

Ysolde waits near the north-side path with her hands in the pockets of a pale coat. She is looking up at the clouds rather than toward the seminar door. When you emerge, she turns.

“The wind is down. The north terrace will be clear for perhaps an hour, and I have brought no book. I thought we could look at the view.”

The path beyond her curves between the garden wall and a row of low dragon-carved arches.

exchanges.player:
